newsitem.title: UK: Britain ups pressure on pension misselling.
newsitem.headline: Britain ups pressure on pension misselling.

text.p: The British government on Wednesday intensified its policy of 'naming and shaming' companies as part of efforts to clear up a four billion pound ($6.8 billion) pension misselling scandal.
The review into the pension misselling scandal was launched by Britain's top financial regulator, the Securities and Investments Board (SIB), three years ago.

As many as 1.5 million people may have been wrongly advised by the financial services industry to take out personal pensions in the late 1980s and early 1990s instead of staying in occupational schemes.
Figures released by the government on Wednesday showed two firms, Hogg Robinson and Colonial, had paid compensation in fewer than one percent of cases.
Hogg Robinson had offered compensation in just two cases and had it accepted in only one.
A spokesman for the company said that it had devoted considerable resources to the pensions review and remained committed to meeting the targets prescribed by the government.

Today's figures showed only two firms among the 24 worst offenders currently being monitored by the government, Guardian Royal Exchange and Barclays Life, had managed to pay out in more than 10 percent of cases.
Companies have been given until the end of the year by the SIB to complete 90 percent of priority cases by the financial regulator. The remainder of cases must be cleared by the end of 1998.
In a parliamentary written answer, Treasury minister Helen Liddell described the volume of cases cleared as "extremely disappointing" and said companies had a great deal more work to do.
"Some appear to have hardly begun," she added.

Sedgwick Group which with Legal & General was the first to be 'named and shamed' last week for failing to recognise the urgency in sorting out the scandal had completed just one percent of its 6,754 cases. Legal & General had completed around six percent of 33,282 cases.
Prudential Corp which has the largest number of cases oustanding, 58,606, had cleared 3,128, around five percent.

Liddell said it was now imperative that all firms which sold personal pensions make serious efforts to improve their performance in clearing caseloads, in the interests of their customers and their own reputations.
She said the government would continue to monitor performance, adding : "I will decide once I have seen some further figures to measure progress what further action may be called for."
